# Incident Report — MTA 2026-01-31 Traffic Analysis Exercise

## Victim Host
| Field | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| IPv4 | **10.1.21.58** | Top local talker in all conversations |
| MAC | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** | ARP binding for 10.1.21.58; matches DHCP request source and link-local (169.254.227.202) fallback address used by the same host |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** | NBNS name registration from 10.1.21.58; DHCP option 12 hostname; matches AD SPN `_ldap._tcp...DESKTOP-ES9F3ML.win11office.com` |
| Domain | win11office.com (NetBIOS `WIN11OFFICE`) | NBNS/DNS SRV records |
| Logged-in user | **gwyatt** | Kerberos `CNameString` in AS-REQ/TGS traffic between 10.1.21.58 and the domain controller 10.1.21.2 |

Local subnet: 10.1.21.0/24. Gateway 10.1.21.1 (MAC 00:04:c1:be:8c:d4). Domain controller 10.1.21.2 (MAC 14:b3:1f:2d:ce:69) — accounts for the largest internal conversation (LDAP/Kerberos/SMB2/DRSUAPI, benign AD chatter).

## Malware Family
**Browser-check-gated commodity credential/browser stealer, delivered via a fake file-hosting lure chain.** No IDS/AV alert file was provided in the evidence set, and the payload download and bulk exfiltration were TLS-encrypted with no available decryption key, so this attribution is **behavioral, not signature-confirmed**. The observed panel design (numeric/hex victim `id` + `token` check-in, `act=log` telemetry submission, server-side archive named `<public-IP>-<hash>.zip`) is consistent with a stealer-as-a-service (Stealc/Vidar/Lumma-class) panel, but I cannot confirm the exact family without a decrypted payload or signature match.

## Delivery and Infection Chain (all times relative to capture start)
1. **t=45.3s** — DNS query for `hiyter.com` (→104.21.22.231), a redirector/lure page.
2. **t=45.8s** — DNS query for `media.megafilehub4.lat` (→104.21.48.156), fake file-host.
3. **t=48.3s** — DNS query for `arch.filemegahab4.sbs` (→104.21.46.67). Immediately followed by a **16 MB TLS download** from 104.21.46.67 lasting 22.4s (t=48.4s–70.7s), fronted through Cloudflare with Encrypted Client Hello (outer SNI `cloudflare-ech.com`, masking the true destination). Size and delivery pattern (fake-file-host naming, ECH obfuscation) are consistent with a dropper/loader package.
4. **t=90.4s** — Contact with `whooptm.cyou` (→62.72.32.156), likely an ad/redirect gate in the same campaign infrastructure.
5. **t=92.3s–103.9s** — Host checks in to the C2 panel at **whitepepper.su (153.92.1.49)**:
   - `GET /api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&agent=Chrome` returns a small HTML page containing JavaScript that fingerprints the browser environment: `navigator` properties, WebGL vendor/renderer (`AMD Radeon R9 200 Series`), canvas fingerprint, WebRTC ICE candidates, audio context, installed plugins.
   - That script `fetch()`s the collected fingerprint back to `.../set_agent?...&act=log` (HTTP 200), then navigates to `about:blank`.
   - The **server's response body to the `act=log` POST reads: `cant open archive 172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip`** — direct evidence the panel expected a separately uploaded stolen-data archive named by the victim's public/NAT IP (172.56.88.98) and failed to process it.
   - The same sequence repeats with `agent=Edge` at t=103s.
   - Immediately after each failed archive-open, large **encrypted TLS sessions to 153.92.1.49:443** occur (1.5 MB, 419 KB, 275 KB, t≈92–124s) — consistent with the host retrying/completing exfiltration of a harvested-data archive over HTTPS. Contents could not be recovered (TLS, no key log).
6. **t=122.8s** — `holiday-forever.cc` (→80.97.160.24) and **t=126.5s** — `communicationfirewall-security.cc` (→104.21.9.36), both TLS/443 only, likely additional redirector/ad infrastructure tied to the same campaign.
7. **No further contact with any of the above malicious IPs after t≈132s**, out of a 619.7s capture — the observed activity is a single infection/check-in burst, not sustained beaconing.

Note: a previous, unrelated analysis session had left a `carved.zip` and extracted "stealer log" files (passwords.txt, cookies/, autofill/, screenshot.jpg) in the shared `/tmp/mta_objs` scratch directory. I verified none of those filenames or contents appear anywhere in this pcap (`grep` for `screenshot.jpg` / `Google Chrome_Network.txt` returned zero matches) and discarded them as contamination — they are **not** used as evidence below.

## Indicators of Compromise

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| C2 endpoint | **153.92.1.49:80** | Plaintext HTTP check-in/fingerprint gate, `/api/set_agent` |
| C2 endpoint | **153.92.1.49:443** | Large encrypted upload sessions immediately following failed archive-open error |
| Domain | **whitepepper.su** | DNS A→153.92.1.49; HTTP Host header |
| URL | `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome` | Frame ~24594, GET, HTTP 200 |
| URL | `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` | Frame 24601, POST, HTTP 200; server error reveals archive name `172.56.88.98-038485b1855ec7a1ba5bbda042ad17a1.zip` |
| URL | `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?...&agent=Edge&act=log` | Frame 25286, POST, HTTP 200, same server behavior |
| Delivery host | **104.21.46.67:443** (arch.filemegahab4.sbs, ECH-fronted via cloudflare-ech.com) | 16 MB TLS session, t=48.4–70.7s |
| Domain | **arch.filemegahab4.sbs** | DNS A→104.21.46.67, 172.67.136.13 |
| Domain | **media.megafilehub4.lat** | DNS A→104.21.48.156 |
| Domain | **hiyter.com** | DNS A→104.21.22.231, 172.67.207.145; initial lure |
| Domain | **whooptm.cyou** | DNS A→62.72.32.156 |
| Domain | **holiday-forever.cc** | DNS A→80.97.160.24 |
| Domain | **communicationfirewall-security.cc** | DNS A→104.21.9.36, 172.67.141.109 |

No `file_name`/`file_hash` IOC could be grounded: the only sizeable payload transfer (104.21.46.67, 16 MB) and the bulk exfil (153.92.1.49:443) were both TLS-encrypted with no decryption material available in this capture.
